e: Nero, the Bloody Poet (Dezső Kosztolányi, 1922)

Kosztolányi's first novel follows Nero from the death of Claudius (AD 54) to his own death (68): how the awkward, verse-writing youth becomes a murderous emperor who turns his power to the service of his art. It appeared in book form in 1922, with a letter from Thomas Mann meant as a preface.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. Most of the novel takes place in the palace; its city settings are rarer and sketchier than in Quo Vadis. The great fire of 64 and the persecution of the Christians do not appear in it at all. Where the novel mentions only a district or a type of building, the stop is at a nearby point shown on the map, and the text says so. The novel's chapters are not numbered, so the chapter title appears in parentheses (in English translation). Each stop ends with a short comparison with the main ancient sources.
The death of Claudius on the Palatine

The novel opens on a sweltering summer afternoon in the Forum Cupidinis, the delicacies market. An old fruit seller looks up at the hill where the aged emperor Claudius now lives in the former house of Tiberius (“Sweltering Heat”).

Up in the palace the empress Agrippina gives the thirsty Claudius water in a gourd, and he falls down dead. Nero, Agrippina's son and Claudius's adopted son, watches it all; his mother does not let him leave the room (“The Miracle”). The next day soldiers carry the youth off from the palace steps and acclaim him emperor (“Young Emperor”).

According to Tacitus and Suetonius, Claudius was poisoned with mushrooms (Annales 12.66–67; Claudius 44); the gourd of water is the novel's version. The Forum Cupedinis was one of the markets around the Forum; its exact location is unknown, and it is not on the map. The stop is the Domus Tiberiana.
Funeral oration in the Forum

At Claudius's funeral Nero delivers the eulogy from the speakers' platform in the Forum; Seneca wrote it for him. The dead man is declared a god (“The Miracle”). Tacitus also records that the speech was Seneca's work, and that the older people noted that Nero was the first emperor who needed someone else's eloquence (Annales 13.3).

Years later, one autumn morning, Seneca comes down to the Forum through the Argiletum, past the row of bookshops, and goes on from there to the steam bath. The novel lists what he sees: the statues of Alcibiades and Marsyas, the back-street lawyers near the sundial, the money changers, and a street boy selling matches in front of the statue of the she-wolf (“Three Poets in the Steam Bath”).

Martial also mentions the booksellers of the Argiletum; the statue of Marsyas really did stand in the Forum. The stop is the Rostra.
Around the Circus Maximus

The Circus Maximus is a recurring setting in the novel. On sleepless nights Nero remembers his childhood: after his father's death he grew up in the house of his aunt Lepida, sharing a room with a dancer who performed in the Circus Maximus (“Night in Labor”). As emperor, dressed as a charioteer, he roams the booths and street girls around the circus at night with the poet Zodicus (“Literary School”).

Later he races himself: according to the novel four hundred thousand people watch him on the track between the Palatine and the Aventine (“The Charioteer”). After Poppaea's death he wanders around the circus and believes he has found the dead woman in a boy named Sporus (“Alone”).

According to Suetonius, the child Nero grew up at his aunt's under the supervision of a dancer and a barber (Nero 6). Tacitus also writes about the night wanderings (Annales 13.25), and according to Suetonius Nero drove a chariot in the Circus Maximus as well (Nero 22). Pliny the Elder puts the circus's capacity at 250,000 (Nat. hist. 36.102).
Night on the Fabrician bridge

The night excursions grow wilder. Nero brings home a wretched dwarf from the outskirts to keep on a chain for the amusement of his guests. Zodicus and Fannius, the two court poets, throw dogs and cats from the Fabrician bridge into the Tiber every night. They make such a racket that the night watch turns out, suspecting a murder (“Wings Grow”).

Meanwhile in the palace Octavia, Nero's fourteen-year-old wife, waits in vain for her husband to come home and listens to the flute playing from the garden.

According to Tacitus, Nero roamed the streets, taverns and brothels at night disguised as a slave, and with his companions also assaulted passers-by (Annales 13.25). The Fabrician bridge, built in 62 BC, is still in use today.
Nero's garden and the death of Britannicus

At dusk Nero likes to sit in the garden by the fountain. From there he can see the slopes of the Esquiline, where there was once a cemetery for the poor until Maecenas had it turned into a promenade (“Doctors at the Sickbed”). Now he cannot work: the voice of his stepbrother Britannicus will not leave his head.

At dawn he walks out to the outskirts to Locusta, the poisoner, and has her brew fresh poison before his eyes. He gives a festive meal and invites Britannicus too. Britannicus finds the wine too hot and asks for cold water; Zodicus pours his own cup into it. The boy's head falls onto the gold plate, and the feast goes on (“Murder”).

Horace also describes the transformation of the cemetery (Satirae 1.8). Britannicus died at an imperial banquet in AD 55; according to Tacitus too, the drink that was too hot was cooled with the poisoned cold water (Annales 13.15–17); according to Suetonius, Locusta brewed the poison in Nero's bedroom, before his eyes (Nero 33). The novel does not name the garden; the stop is the surviving building of the Gardens of Maecenas.
A woman in the audience

Nero goes to the Theater of Marcellus with Epaphroditus, his secretary, and the actor Paris. From a side box he watches the farces and pantomimes, which the people now like better than tragedies (“A Woman in the Audience”).

He is bored, so he watches the audience instead. Down in the stalls, in the rows of the knights, he notices a woman who seems to be looking toward the imperial box. Paris whispers to him that she is Poppaea Sabina, who is there every evening.

According to the sources, Nero met Poppaea through Otho, whose wife she then was (Tacitus, Annales 13.45–46); the meeting at the theater is the novel's invention.
Nero on stage

Poppaea wants Nero to perform before a large audience. They go through the theaters one by one: Balbus's is small, Marcellus's is pretty, Pompey's is very large; according to the novel it holds forty thousand spectators (“Applause”). Seneca and Burrus organize the paid applauders.

Nero first performs at the youth festival, the Juvenalia; he trembles with stage fright all day (“The Divine Actor”). Afterward the companies of the theaters of Pompey, Marcellus and Balbus all send delegations to congratulate him (“Triumph”). Later he also performs in the Theater of Pompey (the chapter “Society of Roman Citharists”).

According to Tacitus, the Juvenalia performance took place in Nero's private theater, and a special troop was organized from the applauders (Annales 14.15). According to Pliny the Elder, Nero had the Theater of Pompey gilded for a single day for the visit of the Armenian king Tiridates (Nat. hist. 33.54). The 4th-century register gives the theater 17,580 places.
Poppaea on the Campus Martius

Poppaea deliberately draws away from Nero so as to bind him more closely to her. She throws him away from her the way a circus juggler throws a hoop: so that it rolls back on its own (“The Hoop That Rolls Back”).

She has herself carried through the Campus Martius, under the Porticus of Octavia, the promenade of high society. In front of the Theater of Marcellus she meets Menecrates, the lyre player, who invites her to his villa. She looks up the actors and writers she has neglected for a while and hears the latest literary gossip.

Menecrates is a real person: according to Suetonius, Nero presented him with the property and houses of generals who had celebrated triumphs (Nero 30).
The Society of Roman Citharists

The Society of Roman Citharists is housed on the Via Appia, in two rooms on an upper floor. It was once a meeting place for musicians; now it is a dicing den for poets and actors who have fallen out of the emperor's favor (the chapter “Society of Roman Citharists”).

Zodicus and Fannius gather here, and here they run down Nero, who these days sings almost every evening in the circus and the theater. Zodicus says the emperor is performing in the Theater of Pompey that day, but that he did not even go.

The society is the novel's invention; the novel does not give the exact location of the house along the Via Appia. The stop is the road's stretch within the city.
Conspiracy at the harbor

At night ships are loading in the Tiber harbor, and the sailors of the fleet at Misenum arrive too. That same night the conspirators led by Piso meet, among them Zodicus and Fannius, who point to the sailors' discontent. The conspirators plan that at the festival of Ceres, when Nero is at the circus, the consul Lateranus will hand him a petition and the others will stab him, as Caesar was once stabbed (“Revolution”).

The conspiracy is uncovered. Seneca is drawn into it too; the emperor condemns him to death. Seneca dies in the bath water, in the presence of a centurion, in the arms of his wife Paulina (“Seneca”).

This is one of the most historical parts of the novel. According to Tacitus, Epicharis tried to win over an officer of the fleet at Misenum, and the assassination was planned for the circus games of the festival of Ceres (Annales 15.51, 15.53). Seneca died at his villa four miles from the city (15.60–64). The novel does not name the harbor; the stop is the Emporium, Rome's main river port.
The colossus in front of the palace

In the first half of the novel, after Corbulo's victory in the East, Nero has the statues of the old emperors removed and sets up his own hundred-foot bronze statue in front of the palace colonnade (“To Forget”). Toward the end of the novel, in the days of the revolt, someone hangs a leather sack on the colossus. Matricides were sewn into such sacks. From this Nero understands that it is the end (“In Phaon's Garden”).

Nero had Agrippina killed years before; the novel tells of it in the chapters “Storm” and “The Best Mother,” beyond the edge of the map, on the seacoast.

According to Suetonius, the 120-foot statue stood in the vestibule of Nero's Golden House, and during the revolt a sack was tied to one of his statues with the inscription: “What could I do? But you deserved the sack” (Nero 31, 45). The colossus was built only after the fire of 64; the novel places it earlier. Hadrian later had it moved next to the Colosseum; the site of its base is shown separately on the map.
Flight from the city

At night Epaphroditus wakes Nero: the soldiers have deserted him, and people are speaking of Galba as emperor. Nero puts on a charioteer's clothes, takes Britannicus's old lyre, and flees the palace with Sporus and his secretary through a gap broken in a wall (“In Phaon's Garden”).

They come out onto the Palatine, then walk in the dark along the bank of the Tiber, stumbling over corpses. Fires flare up on the Pincian and the Vatican. Until dawn they meet no one on the olive-lined road.

The novel names no gate. The Via Salaria started at the Porta Collina of the Servian wall; according to Suetonius, Nero fled on horseback, barefoot, his face covered, with four companions, and passed the camp of the guard (Nero 48).
In Phaon's garden

On the Via Salaria, not far from the city, lives Phaon, a freedman who once worked in the imperial treasury and has retired to farming. At his gate a fugitive in charioteer's clothes, with a stubbly chin, asks to be let in: the emperor (“In Phaon's Garden”).

By evening the soldiers arrive. In a shed Nero tries to kill himself with his stage sword but cannot; in the end Epaphroditus, out of pity, presses his head onto it. After his death his old nurse, Ecloge, arrives from Rome, washes him, laments him in Greek, and puts an obol for Charon in his mouth (“Lament”).

According to Suetonius, Phaon's villa lay between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, around the fourth milestone, beyond the edge of the map. As he died, Nero said: “What an artist perishes with me!” His nurses Egloge and Alexandria, together with Acte, buried him in the tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian Hill (Nero 48–50).
